description: We are physics engineers who love astronomy and programming.
summary:
DynoSPHEREx is a web application for observing the same area of ​​the sky on different dates. It allows users to search for astronomical images, play them back as a sequence, and identify objects that may be changing position.

The observations accessed come from the NASA/IPAC IRSA public archive and are part of the SPHEREx mission. Users can also upload their own files. The application distinguishes between these two sources and retains information to track the origin of each image. It enables the viewing of the complete stellar map and spectral analysis.
details:
1 Objetives

• Create a public web tool that displays sky images from space mission

SPHEREx to make it easy for anyone to see it’s time evolution.

• Show a short video of the region of space delimited by the user by inputting

right ascension (RA) and declination (Dec).

• Facilitate to spot moving objects.

2 Introduction

Planet X is a hypotetical planet that, if it existed, it would orbit the Sun at a

distance 20 to 30 times larger than Neptune’s orbit. It’s existence would help

to explain the unique orbits of small objects in the Kuiper Belt [1]. Some of

the world’s most powerful telescopes are searching for this planet. If it exists, a

complete survey of the sky showing its evolution over time would help provide

visual evidence of it.

Latest telescopes, as SPHEREx, take a lot of observations and the amount of

data is so large that no person or computer code could possibly understand it.[2].

The development of new data analysis will be fundamental for the understanding

of obtained data and the discovery of new celestial bodys.

SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reion-

ization, and Ices Explorer) is an space probe that will collect data on more than

450 million galaxies, along with 100 million stars in the Milky Way, with the

aim of exploring the origins of the universe. [2]

The observatory was launched on March 11, 2025, with the goal of mapping the

sky in the optical spectrum and near-infrared light.[3] It takes 600 exposures

per day, which can be combined to form a mosaic of the entire sky. Each region

of the sky is photographed 102 times, each time with a different color filter [4].

SPHEREx data are publicly available through one data release (dr1) and two

quick releases (qr2 and qr3). Due to the probe’s high imaging rate, we once

again face the problem of having too much data to process. That is why a tool

was developed to help visualize the temporal evolution of this data, which could

allow anyone to easily discover moving objects.

3 Prodecure

3.1 Data handling

A Python script was written that performs a query using the Fast API to access

SPHEREx data stored in IRSA (Infrared Science Archive). [5], [6] This script

takes right ascension and declination values and searches for the FITS images

corresponding to that region of space, displaying them in a loop to generate a

short video, which facilitates the detection of moving objects. In addition, our

code has access to the SIMBAD catalog [7], which allows us to display which

objects are recorded in the selected region. It also connects to the Aladin Sky

Atlas to generate an interactive map of the sky.

SPHEREx spectrophotometry data are utilized, as we display a spectral dia-

gram of the region of study and allow users to overlay FITS files and adjust

transparency to make comparisons even easier.

3.2 Web Development

Recognizing the strengths and weaknesses of different programming languages,

we decided to use Docker to combine the ease of working with databases (espe-

cially when that data is for scientific computing and, in particular, astronomical

computing thanks to astopy) with the speed and visual appeal that JavaScript

and HTML provide for a good user interface. Our process is detailed below:

3.2.1 Backend

The backend is built with FastAPI and runs on Uvicorn. All the scientific

logic resides in a single module, and the API exposes a set of REST endpoints

that the frontend consumes directly.

The main workflow begins when the user requests observations for a set of

coordinates: the backend queries the IRSA archive using the TAP protocol and

returns the list of available products. When the user generates a sequence, the

server downloads the FITS frames one by one, validates them against their pixel

masks (FLAGS and VARIANCE), reprojects them onto a common grid using

the World Coordinate System (WCS), and saves both the original FITS file

and a PNG image for visualization. Sequences are persisted to disk and can be

retrieved by ID, allowing users to share a direct link to a previous session.

The comparison lab receives two frames and evaluates whether they are scientif-

ically comparable: it requires different, known epochs, complete coverage, and

local spectral compatibility. If the rules are met, it calculates the exploratory

difference pixel by pixel and returns it as a PNG and as a FITS file with a doc-

umented header. Additionally, moving objects can be detected by comparing

the centroids of the brightest sources between frames, and their proper motion

can be estimated in arcseconds per year.

3.2.2 Frontend

The frontend is built with React 19 and TypeScript, compiled with Vite 8

and styled with Tailwind CSS 4. All of the interface’s logic resides in a single

App component, reflecting a deliberately compact approach.

The interface is organized into five sections: a coordinate panel for searching

regions of the sky or selecting challenge targets; a time viewer with an animated

player and real-time self-motion detection; the observation catalog with filters

by date, collection, and wavelength; the ChronoSpectral Lab for comparing two

epochs side-by-side, in blink mode, or with overlays; and a traceability panel

showing the source, date, units, and SHA-256 of each FITS file.

No state management or graphics libraries are used: state is managed with

native React hooks, and requests are handled using the browser’s fetch API.

The interactive sky viewer is integrated via an iframe from Aladin Lite v3

(CDS Strasbourg).

4 Conclusions

Our program is an easy-to-use, publicly available web tool that shows users

a short video of the region near the specified coordinates using data from

SPHEREx. For this reason, we conclude that the challenge’s objective has been

met. In addition, a real-time star map was added, along with access to SIM-

BAD and a spectral diagram display, making it one of the most comprehensive

programs for visualizing astronomical data.

We believe the developed tool during this challenge completion helps facilitate

researchers work and, at the same time, is appealing and user-friendly so that

everyone can use it.
